little-sailboat: No full line now: row 4's 4 3 is the only exact fit (4+1+3 = 8). It spends the lone 1s of columns 1 and 8, so their X's leave row 6's 6 exactly six cells; column 5's 3 3 (3+1+3 = 7) stands the mast, with the boom's gap at row 4.
lighthouse: No full line: the rock is a 7 in nine. The only exact fits are columns 3 and 4 — 5 1 2 is 5+1+1+1+2 = 10, the full height — so the tower stands first; row 2's 4 3 then overlaps beside it and the rock settles under the tower.
sand-bucket: A small calm one: row 3's 6 1 fills all eight (6+1+1) — rim and spade — and column 8's 6 is the spade top to bottom. Columns 3-4's 1 4 fit exactly too: handle, gap, bucket. Three easy passes.
anchor: Row 7's 2 2 2 1 — flukes, shaft and rope — fills all ten with its gaps; nothing else is exact. Row 4's 7 1 overlaps around it, the rope's 7 must come down column 10 to meet it, and the right fluke stops a row short (row 6), so the arms are read one by one.
sandcastle: Row 8's 6 2 leaves one spare cell, so the sand doesn't settle column 4 by itself: its 6 still covers columns 2-6, so column 4's lone 1 is the sand and the rest of column 4 is X — a wall you deduce, not read. The castle's 3s fit left of it, the parasol right.
sleeping-fox: Row 5's 4 4 fills all nine with the notch at column 5, but row 4's notches sit at columns 4 and 7 — no mirror — so each half is read from its own columns. Column 1's 4 grows up from row 5 to the tail tip at row 2; the ears are only reachable from columns 7 and 8.
barn-owl: The perch is mid-board now: row 7's 9 in ten overlaps eight cells. Column 9's lone 1 is that branch, so the rest of column 9 is paper and the twig in row 6 must come from column 10; the owl grows up from the perch while its tail hangs below it.
acorn: A breather with a new shape: a swallow in flight. Row 3's 3 1 3 fills all nine — two wings and the body between them — and column 5's 3 3 (head, gap, tail) fits the seven rows exactly; the forked tail and the wing tips follow in four easy passes.
pine-tree: Row 6's 10 in eleven inks nine. The lower boughs are hollow (rows 7-9 read 2 2, 3 5, 3 3), so they are partial rows: column 7's 5 1 1 1 threads the trunk through their gaps, and each bough is placed by its own columns.
wandering-bear: The belly is open now: rows 4 and 5 read 5 4 and 4 4, so the body has a gap. Column 10's 1 8 fits exactly (ear to foot) and opens the board; row 5's 4 4 and column 6's 3 5 then fix where the belly gap sits.
twin-cherries: Rows 6 and 7 read red 5, red 3: same colours need a gap, so 5+1+3 fills all nine. The contrast is row 5 — red 3, green 1, green 1: the left stem's green touches its red cherry with no gap, because different colours may touch.
bunch-carrot: Row 5 reads orange 1, green 1, orange 4: colour order alone decides it — the stalk's green cell must sit between an orange cell and the long orange run, and column 4 is the only column with green that low. Row 2's green 4, green 3 needs a gap and fills all eight.
sunny-lemon: A breather: row 4's red 1, gold 2, red 3, gold 3, red 1 — colours touch — fills all ten at once. The envelope is thin, and the basket's gold band (red 3, gold 1, red 2) is decided by the same rule in one look. Four passes.
ice-cream-cone: Column 7 is the drip line: pink 1, 1, 1, 1 down ten cells, and its gaps reach four rows — rows 5, 7 and 9 end in a pink drop while rows 4, 6 and 8 stop short. Columns 3-4 (pink 4, brown 5 and 6) stand the cone first; the drips are placed from column 7.
hall-bronze-bell: Bigger bell, and a void decides a run: column 4's 1 6 is cut by the void in row 2, and the 6 needs every cell below it — so the 1 can only be the beam in row 1. Row 9's 2 4 3 fills all eleven (the lip), and the clapper swings right, so each column is read on its own.
marble-bust: The face is open now: eyes, nose and mouth leave rows 3-7 as partial lines (3 4, 1 2 4, 6 3, 4 2, 2 3). Columns 5, 6 and 8 fit exactly between the voids (6 6, 2 3 6, 8 4) and stand the head; each face row is then placed against them, and row 11's 11 squares the shoulders.
lidded-urn: A calm one with a new silhouette: a pagoda whose spire sits right of centre, so the voids differ side to side. The first move is a column: column 7's 3 4 1 fills all ten (spire, upper storey, base). Row 8's 9 then fills every framed cell between its void and the edge, and the eaves of row 5 overhang to the left.
bronze-mina: Void and colour together: columns 3 and 8 read umber 5, umber 4, teal 2 — the void corners above and the plinth below leave exactly that many cells, so both fill and their paper gap in row 6 is the neck. The teal plinth is 9 and 8 wide in 11 and 10 cells — one spare each — so its edge comes from the columns, not the rows.
sunflower-head: Columns 6 and 7 read gold 2, umber, gold 1, sage 4 — colours touch — and fill first. The seed head is no solid block: paper seeds in rows 4-6 make the umber disc partial lines, so each petal and seed cell is gold or umber only where its row and column both allow it.
festival-kite: Row 5 is smudged and lopsided: coral then gold on the left, gold then coral on the right, a gap at column 4. No mirror copy helps — each column paints its own row-5 cell; column 4's gold 4, gold 2 needs its gap exactly there, under row 4's gold 8 spar.
festival-candle: Row 7 is smudged. A halo of gold sparks and a holder with a handle frame the candle: column 5's gold 4, coral 4, gold 2 fills all ten (flame, wick and wax, holder), and row 9's gold 7, gold 1 places the handle; the wax columns carry coral through the hidden row.
weather-vane: One foothold: column 5's 8 in ten overlaps rows 3-8. Row 6's lone 1 is then that pole cell, so the rest of row 6 is paper — a wall of X's that splits the vane from the roof. From that wall the chain runs both ways: the rooster and arrow above, the roof's 7 below.
stargazer-hat: Practise the chain with colour, given two ways in: row 9's brim fills and row 8's 3 4 leaves one spare cell in nine, so six of its cells are sure. Column 1's 2 is then the brim, column 2's 2 drops below the gold band, so row 6's 6 sits in columns 3-8 and the cone chains up to the tip.
moon-rover: A calm one with one clear reveal: row 6's grey 2, sky 6, grey 2 — colours touch — is the window strip and fills all ten. Row 5's 2 4 2 and the wheel row's 2 2 2 1 fit exactly too, so the chassis is laid in three lines; panel and antenna follow.
exhibit-mina-portrait: A calm one: rows 5-7 fill the width exactly — row 6's wink is the only paper in the face. The beret's band has a notch (row 3: teal 5, teal 2 in nine), so it is no full line: column 7 tells you where the notch sits.
astronaut-helmet: Row 12's 2 7 2 fits exactly, and columns 7 and 8 fill all thirteen cells because colours touch; that spine through the visor carries the chain out to the rim. A glint of paper in the visor (row 4) and a gap in the boots (row 11) keep the rim from filling by itself — each side is read from its own columns.
watermelon-slice: Read the rind from the columns: column 4's red 1, red 4, teal 1 and column 5's red 6, teal 1 place the flesh down to the rind first. Row 3 no longer fits exactly (red 4, red 3 in eleven), so each rind cell in rows 2-5 is the teal edge its column ends on — column 1's teal 3 and column 11's teal 2 hold the two sides.
striped-awning: Row 2's red 3, cream 3, red 3, cream 1 fills all ten — colours touch. The stripes are not mirrored: row 3's right red stripe is cut short (red 1 after a gap), a partial row only the columns can place; row 9's cream 10 is the counter and columns 2 and 9 stand the posts.
apple-basket: Start from the basket: row 6's brown 10 rim and row 7's weave 1 2 2 2 fill outright and settle column 1. The apples are no longer one exact row (row 5 reads red 2, red 3, red 2 with a spare cell), so each apple is placed by its own column — red only where that column's clue still holds red.
ionic-capital: The volute's eye (row 5, column 6) is cut out of the canvas — a void. Row 5's 2 1 1 1 loses a cell to slide in and column 6's 3 1 1 must step around the hole. Row 2's 11 and columns 3 and 9 (2 1 6) fill outright; rows 7 and 11 then overlap and the flutes settle.
firefly-jar: Column 3 is smudged, but one firefly in it is stamped (row 6): it anchors the hidden column. Row 1's gold 1 6 1 fills all ten and columns 5 and 7 fit; row 6's night 2, gold 1, night 7 has its firefly given, and the rest of column 3 is read row by row from the crossings.
kiln-willow-plate: Bound the ? with a wall: rows 4 and 6 settle first, and column 8's night 6 is the willow's trunk from the rim down to row 6 — so row 5's cream ? runs from the rim to that trunk: columns 2-7, 6. The willow leans right and the bridge sits low left, so nothing mirrors.
paper-boat: Row 7 is smudged. The sky is trimmed to five rows; row 5's gold 1, coral 6, coral 5 and row 6's gold 13 deck fill first. Columns 1 and 13 (the lantern strings) decide whether the hidden row touches the edges, and every other column counts down through it.
laurel-wreath: Twist: the void heart cuts rows 4-8 into pockets, and the right-hand leaves are partial (rows 3, 5 and 9 break), so the wreath is no mirror. Column 3's 2 1 4 fills all nine framed cells between its voids exactly; the right side is then chained row by row from the pockets.
mosaic-elephant: Row 4's 2 8 fills all eleven exactly; the stamped gap in row 6 caps column 4's 5 at rows 1-5, splitting trunk from leg, and the chain runs on in five passes.
mosaic-seahorse: The stamp pins a run: column 2's 3 2 1 fits exactly (3+1+2+1+1 = 8) and sets the back, and the stamped tile in row 5 sits inside that row's 4, so the 4 can't slide past it — it lands on columns 2-5. The tail curls out across the right half from there.
